findings.summary: Code block appears after the options table, and the key idea 'one Pool per process' is stated only after the code, so the code is not preceded by its one-line idea.
findings.evidence:
javascript
// db.js: created once at startup ... One Pool per process
findings.fix: State 'One Pool per process, created at startup' as a bullet before the code block, then show the code.

findings.summary: The lifecycle (Acquire, Query, Release) and the full-pool outcome are split between a diagram and loose bullets, so the queue-or-timeout branch is text rather than part of the visual.
findings.evidence: All clients busy: requests queue until one frees / Or the acquire timeout fires and the request errors
findings.fix: Add a branch to the lifecycle diagram showing 'pool full: queue, then timeout error' and drop the two bullets.

findings.summary: The transaction code block repeats Page 3 and appears before its idea is stated; the one-line idea 'dedicated client for a transaction' comes after the code.
findings.evidence: const client = await pool.connect(); ... dedicated client for a transaction
findings.fix: Replace the code with a one-line pointer to the Transactions page, or state the idea before the code.

findings.summary: A bullet holds two ideas: the ORDER BY row mixes direction with the identifiers rule, and the Mistakes section crams the injection point and its 'looks safe' caveat together.
findings.evidence: WHERE id = ${id} is SQL injection, even if the value 'looks' safe
findings.fix: Split into separate bullets: 'Never interpolate values with ${}' and 'Injection applies even to values that look safe'.

findings.summary: The Prisma/Drizzle table has 'n/a' cells that are unclear: Drizzle 'Batch' and 'Timeout' n/a gives no information on what to use instead.
findings.evidence: Batch | $transaction([op1, op2]) | n/a ; Timeout | default 5s | n/a
findings.fix: Replace 'n/a' with the actual Drizzle behaviour (e.g. 'use db.batch' or 'no default timeout') or drop the rows.

findings.summary: Page repeats the pg transaction code identical to pages 2 and 6, and the pg code appears before the idea is stated about the pattern.
findings.fix: Keep the full code only here and reference it from pages 2 and 6.

findings.summary: The code block shows two examples (Prisma then Drizzle) with a caption placed after the code instead of an idea before it.
findings.fix: Label each line with a comment (// Prisma, // Drizzle) and state in one line before the code that both fetch active users.

findings.summary: The section does not cover an outline point (missing "injection", "straight").
findings.evidence: Mistake: passing user input straight into a filter allows operator injection (e.g. { password: { $ne: null } }); validate that values are plain strings and be cautious with $where
findings.fix: Add the point with an explanation and an example.

findings.summary: The shutdown sequence is described as a diagram but 'Hangs' and process.exit are placed as loose nodes, and the callout duplicates page 6.
findings.evidence: Stop intake / Release clients / Close pools / Exit ... Hangs
findings.fix: Make the shutdown a single ordered flow and keep the 'pool.end() waits' warning only once.

findings.summary: A bullet holds two ideas: the MongoClient bullet combines one-client-per-process with the built-in pool size.
findings.evidence: One MongoClient per process; the pool is built in (maxPoolSize 100)
findings.fix: Split into 'One MongoClient per process' and 'Pool is built in; maxPoolSize defaults to 100'.

findings.summary: Shutdown order is inconsistent with page 5: page 5 lists releasing clients as its own step, page 6 omits it, and 'Stop server' vs 'Stop intake' name the same step differently.
findings.evidence: Stop server / no new requests / Close DB ... vs Stop intake / SIGTERM / SIGINT / Release clients
findings.fix: Use the same step names on both pages and include the release-clients step in the cheat sheet.
